item.title: Microsoft publishes open-source Model Context Protocol curriculum and Qdrant memory server
item.description:
Microsoft publishes open-source Model Context Protocol curriculum and Qdrant memory server

Microsoft has released an open-source curriculum for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) alongside an official MCP server for Qdrant, enabling developers to build modular, secure AI workflows and implement semantic memory layers using specific language examples and vector search integration.

🧩 The MCP Curriculum

The new open-source curriculum introduces the fundamentals of MCP through real-world, cross-language examples. It is designed for developers to learn practical techniques for building modular, scalable, and secure AI workflows, covering everything from session setup to service orchestration.

  • Languages Covered: C#, Java, JavaScript, Rust, Python, and TypeScript.
  • Repository: The resources are hosted at https://github.com/microsoft/mcp-for-beginners.git.
  • Global Accessibility: The repository includes more than 50 language translations. Note that these translations significantly increase the download size.
  • Community Support: Developers can join the Microsoft Foundry Discord community using the provided link.

🧠 The Qdrant MCP Server

The release includes an official Model Context Protocol server for keeping and retrieving memories in the Qdrant vector search engine. This server acts as a semantic memory layer on top of the Qdrant database and is based on FastMCP.

Core Tools

  • qdrant-store: Stores information in the Qdrant database.
  • qdrant-find: Retrieves relevant information from the Qdrant database.

Configuration Details

Configuration is handled via environment variables, and the only command-line argument is --transport, which selects the transport protocol. You cannot provide both QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH simultaneously.

Environment Variable Description
QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH Path to the local Qdrant database (alternative to QDRANT_URL)
EMBEDDING_PROVIDER Embedding provider to use (currently only “fastembed” is supported)
EMBEDDING_MODEL Name of the embedding model to use
QDRANT_SEARCH_LIMIT Maximum number of results to return from search
QDRANT_READ_ONLY Enable read-only mode (disables qdrant-store tool)
FASTMCP_HOST Host address to bind the server to (SSE and HTTP transports)
FASTMCP_PORT Port to run the server on (SSE and HTTP transports)
FASTMCP_MASK_ERROR_DETAILS Hide exception details from tool error messages sent to clients

Naming Conventions

Before version 0.9.0, settings used the FASTMCP_SERVER_ prefix (e.g., FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST). The old names FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST, FASTMCP_SERVER_PORT, and FASTMCP_SERVER_DEBUG still work but are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. If both old and new names are set, the new name takes precedence.

🚀 Availability and Usage

The mcp-server-qdrant can be run directly without specific installation steps by using uvx. The server supports different transport protocols specified using the --transport flag.

#MCP #Microsoft #Qdrant #AIDevelopment #OpenSource

Source: microsoft/mcp-for-beginners Source: qdrant/mcp-server-qdrant

item.title: Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes
item.description:
Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes

The Weaviate Helm chart has released version 17.1.0, introducing significant updates to cluster bootstrapping in Weaviate v1.25 and removing default resource constraints to improve module performance.

🔍 Overview

Weaviate can be deployed to a Kubernetes cluster using the provided Helm chart, provided that Helm is installed. Version 17.1.0 of the chart addresses specific infrastructure changes required by newer Weaviate releases and resolves performance restrictions in default configurations.

⚙️ Key Details: Cluster Bootstrapping

Weaviate v1.25 introduced a significant change in how the cluster bootstraps, driven by the adoption of a Raft-based consensus model.

  • The podManagementPolicy was changed from OrderedReady to Parallel.
  • This change is required for the Raft cluster to bootstrap properly, as all pods must start simultaneously.
  • Once the Raft cluster is established, rolling updates are possible.
  • This change takes effect when migrating from versions prior to v1.25 or when bootstrapping a new v1.25 cluster.

⚠️ Migration Steps

When upgrading from a version older than v1.25 to v1.25 or above, the following one-time operation is required:

  1. Delete Weaviate’s Statefulset.
  2. Update the Statefulset settings to reflect the new policy.

This process will not remove your data but is necessary to make the update of Statefulset settings possible.

📉 Key Details: Resource Limits

In Weaviate-Helm version 17.1.0, the default resource limits and requests defined in the values.yml file have been removed.

  • Reason: Previous default values restricted the performance of some modules, making them almost unusable unless resources.requests and resources.limits were overridden.
  • Impact: Modules deployed with default values prior to version 17.1.0 will have their resource values removed upon upgrading to 17.1.0 or above, resulting in no constraints on memory or CPU usage.
  • Recommendation: To prevent modules from consuming all system resources, users are strongly recommended to override modules.$MODULE.resources.requests and modules.$MODULE.resources.limits with values that suit their specific system.

🛠 Release Process

To release a new version of the chart, the following steps are taken:

  • Bump the chart version in ./weaviate/Chart.yaml.
  • Create a commit and an annotated tag matching the version number (prefixed with v, e.g., v1.4.3).
  • Push the commit and tag to the repository.
  • A GitHub Action creates a drafted release with the packaged chart attached.
  • The draft is edited to include release notes and published.

#Weaviate #Kubernetes #Helm #VectorDB #DevOps

Source: weaviate/weaviate-helm

item.title: Qdrant Vector Search Tutorial Collection Released
item.description:
Qdrant Vector Search Tutorial Collection Released

A new collection of examples and tutorials has been released for the Qdrant vector search engine. The repository contains a curated set of tutorials, demos, and how-to guides focused on Qdrant and adjacent technologies.

🧩 How it works

The tutorials cover a range of data types and use cases, including:

  • Text Data: Introduction to the intersection of vector databases and natural language processing.
  • Image Data: Use of semantic search for accurate skin cancer image comparison with Qdrant and CLIP.
  • Audio Data: Introduction to audio embeddings, audio data, and music recommendation systems.
  • Agentic RAG: Building a vector-search-powered agentic workflow to extract insights from meeting recordings using Qdrant and CrewAI.

⚙️ Key details

Specific guides within the collection include:

  • “Qdrant 101 - Getting Started”: Introduction to semantic search and the recommendation API of Qdrant.
  • “Build a Semantic Search Engine in 5 Minutes”: A quick starter tutorial that builds a semantic search engine for science-fiction books.
  • “Semantic Search for Sci-Fi Books”: A demonstration of semantic search over a top-100 set of science-fiction books.
  • “Build a Semantic Search API”: A guide to searching startup descriptions by meaning with Qdrant Cloud Inference, filtering by city, and serving results through FastAPI.
  • “Language Model QA with Qdrant”: A tutorial on document retrieval with Vision Language Models and binary quantization.
  • “AI Getting Started Demo”: A sample menu dataset and pre-written script used by the “Start building on Qdrant” agent prompt in the Qdrant docs to demo local semantic search.

💡 Why it matters

The collection provides structured learning paths for developers, covering foundational concepts such as the recommendation API and advanced implementations like agentic workflows and visual document retrieval.

#Qdrant #VectorSearch #SemanticSearch #RAG #Tutorials #CLIP

Source: qdrant/examples

item.title: Knowhere Provides Milvus’s C++ Vector Search Core
item.description:
Knowhere Provides Milvus’s C++ Vector Search Core

Knowhere is an independent C++ project that serves as Milvus’s internal core for vector search, integrating FAISS, HNSW and DiskANN. It can be built as part of Milvus or developed as a library, with CPU and GPU build options.

🔍 Overview

Knowhere acts as Milvus’s internal vector search engine. For users who want to use it within Milvus without modifying Knowhere’s source code, the project recommends building Milvus directly; Knowhere is then built implicitly.

⚙️ Platforms and dependencies

All Linux distributions are available for Knowhere development. Most contributors work on Ubuntu or CentOS, with a smaller group using Mac systems on x86_64 or Apple Silicon.

The project lists these verified operating systems for building and running Knowhere:

Operating system Details
Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64 and Aarch64
Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64 and Aarch64; kept for legacy reasons, with EOL by April 2025
macOS x86_64 and Apple Silicon

The scripts/install_deps.sh script installs dependencies for building, testing and shipping the Knowhere library.

🖥️ Build options

GPU support is disabled by default. Setting WITH_GPU=True enables Cardinal GPU support when building with Cardinal, or cuVS otherwise. WITH_CUVS=True explicitly enables cuVS, including alongside Cardinal, independently of WITH_GPU.

GPU builds use CUDA 13.2 for both cuVS and Cardinal. CMake prepares the toolkit before enabling CUDA, including when Knowhere is built through add_subdirectory. An existing toolkit at /usr/local/cuda-13.2 is reused. If it is absent, scripts/install_cuda.sh installs it on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, on x86_64 or Aarch64, and requires root access or passwordless sudo. Other systems must prepare the toolkit at that path beforehand. A GPU device or driver is not needed to compile, and the build must be reconfigured when switching CUDA versions. CPU builds do not invoke the CUDA installer.

Common build commands include:

Build Command
CPU release (default) make
GPU release with cuVS make WITH_GPU=True
GPU release with Cardinal make WITH_CARDINAL=True WITH_GPU=True
CPU with unit tests make WITH_UT=True
CPU unit tests with AddressSanitizer make WITH_UT=True WITH_ASAN=True
GPU with unit tests make WITH_GPU=True WITH_UT=True
Debug build make WITH_DEBUG=True
C ABI and Java JNI bindings with C tests make WITH_JNI=True WITH_C_API_TESTS=True
Custom compiler through a Conan profile make CONAN_PROFILE=clang14

Building a Python wheel requires swig and Python development headers, such as python3-dev on Ubuntu. A portable manylinux wheel can be built with make wheel.

🔌 Bindings and contributions

Optional C ABI and Java 11 JNI bindings expose indexes, brute-force search and named index blobs without a framework dependency. The Java bindings are documented in java/README.md.

Before submitting a pull request, contributors can install and enable pre-commit hooks with pip3 install pre-commit and pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type pre-push. They can run all hooks with make pre-commit, or run formatting and linting separately with make format and make lint. The lint command uses clang-tidy and requires a prior build. If clang-format and clang-tidy are not installed, the project provides installation instructions for Linux and Mac.

#Knowhere #Milvus #VectorSearch #C++ #CUDA

Source: zilliztech/knowhere
